subject: next step for bird-friendly building ordinance?
comment: Dear Councilman Dugan: Thank you for your continuing support of the Bird Window Collision Working Group from Great Salt Lake Audubon. As you recall, we are trying to get Salt Lake City to amend building standards so that new construction projects adopt bird-friendly windows and design. You led the Salt Lake City Council to a unanimous straw vote in favor of bird-friendly window standards, with requests for additional detail. Since then, we have met with Kelsey Lindquist and Amy Thompson, Planning Managers with SLC, who were very helpful. They provided a number of questions, which we have tried to address with a draft ordinance, a background document that fleshes out the ordinance with research, and an evolving FAQ document (attached, along with a pdf of this letter). We also agreed to work closely with planning; we can provide any research or responses as needed. Ms. Thompson and Ms. Lindquist said we would need to get the council and staff to communicate some sort of priority for this work to the planning staff. They suggested we reach out to Brian Fullmer and Nick Tarbet, and perhaps Rachel Otto. I wanted to link you in first, to update you and see if you had any additional questions. In addition, I want to confirm with you the suggested process. Should we provide this information to all three of them at once? Is there an order you would suggest? We appreciate your efforts to enhance the broader sustainability achievements of Salt Lake City. Sincerely yours, Barbara Brown Barbara Brown Member, Bird Window Collision Working Group Great Salt Lake Audubon

subject: The Great Salt Lake
comment: Hello Council member Dugan, My name is Owen Morris. I am senior at East High School, and I am writing to you about a concern that has been growing in recent years, that being the water rights of our home Utah. Everywhere I turn I hear doom and gloom about the future of the Great Salt Lake and the water usage of Utah. I like to think of myself as an optimist, but I only seem to hear about the bad and none of the good. I am at the point in my life where I am leaving home and deciding what I want to do with the rest of my life, and I must decide if my future lies in Utah or elsewhere. If in the near future when I am an adult and I cannot access the basic human necessity of water, or if the Great Salt Lake has dried up and rendered Salt Lake City uninhabitable, then I will be forced to leave the slopes, the red rock, the trails, my friends and family. I would have to leave my home. I don't want this to happen. I want to live in this great state for the rest of my life. I urge you to invest in water conservation and to create goals for the Great Salt Lake's elevation levels, and to allow more water to return to the Lake instead of diverting to industries that only provide economic gain. I believe that the lives of the people living in Utah and their access to water is of greater import than the economic gain to be had by sacrificing our precious water. Please think of the people and help save our Lake. Sincerely, Owen Morris

subject: U baseball land lease
comment: Dan, I continue to find it impossible to provide comment on the physical limitations of the site for a baseball stadium absent verified ALTA topographic mapping, cross-sections of retention walls and related elevation drawings from the U. I seriously question that SLC Engineering and Public Utilities do not also share this concern. No verifiable review has been conducted, as is otherwise required for basic planning approvals in SLC. I understand from second-hand conversations with those who have seen Tyler Murdock's "public benefits" analysis that it has only become available within 24 hours of the Council's vote to approve the land lease. This is absurd. Although I've not seen it, Tyler apparently believes the right field wall, after consummation of the lease will be 29' in height, a mere 8% reduction relative to the 35' version on existing U land. Given available aerial topography, the retention wall at left field will be a minimum of 22-24' high. The ONLY reason for extending left field into Sunnyside Park is to enable spectator seating on the right field line as the existing practice field home is arbitrarily moved 93°. This contradicts prior assertions presented to the community by the U. Sufficient distance re. NCAA standards is in place without the need for a lease or land sale. Other statements by Robin Burt to the YNC have also proven to be mistruths. The Council's assertion that the city will continue to own the property appears to enable a loophole to satisfy the BLM's requirement to perpetuate public recreational use. Regardless of ownership status, the NCAA has prohibited public use of the practice field despite the U's past promises to the community. Nothing will, or can change this. Impacts due to storm runoff from synthetic turf have not been adequately evaluated. FieldTurf contains carcinogens. The city administration did not require RHSM's contractor to adhere to the approved storm water retention vault. This resulted in flooding at East HS and unprecedented taxpayer expense. Commercial vending of concessions, fan apparel, and other goods contradicts the intent of open space zoning regardless of whatever loopholes the Council may concede. If the Council really believes master plans, especially recent ones like for the East Bench have any pertinence, now would be the time to validate. The community's mutual efforts with the U to produce that document cannot be arbitrarily discarded. Your constituents have an absolute and critical reliance upon the integrity of their representatives. Please share these concerns with your fellow council members. Respectfully, James Webster, RLA plate

subject: 90 day reprieve from approval of land transfer from sunnyside Park to UU
comment: Dear Councilman Dugan I am sharing my letter to Jessica Wade, the SLC Field Manager of the Bureau of Land Management with you regarding a land transfer from the BLM to SLC/University of Utah as part of the proposed UU baseball stadium project. I hope you can appreciate the concern about the lack of transparency, adequate information and public process in this action. Respectfully Lynn K. Pershing Ms. Jessica Wade SLC Field Manager Bureau of Land Management [redacted-email] Dear Jessica, I am Lynn K. Pershing, President of K.E.E.P. Yalecrest, a nonprofit 501 3c, whose mission is to "Keep Educating and Encouraging Preservation of Yalecrest" and registered on the Salt Lake City list of Recognized Community Organizations (RCO). I am writing in support of the Friends of Sunnyside Park. It has come to my attention that a section of land involved in a proposed land lease agreement between the City of Salt Lake and the University of Utah is under the control of the Department of Interior, Bureau of Land Management (Source: BLM land patent #43-90-0014, signed February 16, 1990, pursuant to the original Act of June 14, 1926). As such, neither the city nor University is currently authorized to consummate this agreement. I am writing to request you to set a 90 day reprieve on any decision by the Salt Lake City Council to grant a transfer of that land from the BLM to the City or University of Utah until further information on the proposed University of Utah baseball stadium project is provided to the public. Currently, that land is part of city public open lands (Sunnyside Park). The ambiguity about the baseball stadium project versus the original intent for this land to be used to create an extension to the existing Salt Lake Sports Complex (previously named the Steiner Aquatic Center) by City approved East Bench Master Plan (1987, 2017) dictates more information before finalization. Information required for before any land transfer should include 1-Fulfillment of the GRAMA requests by citizen groups to the University of Utah regarding this project. 2-Complete elevations of the proposed project depicting wall heights on all sides of the facility, facility heights, overhead lighting, sound system and score board size and location as well as the height of tall safety nets around the perimeter. To date only aerial views of its boundaries have been provided to any entity. Despite the City's prepared justification of a land lease to the University of Utah in their public benefits document, I believe that providing a below-market ground lease for the Parcel as a 124 stall parking lot is an INappropriate use of City resources to achieve the City's and District 6 goals and does NOT enhance the safety, health, prosperity, moral well-being, peace, order, comfort, or convenience of the vast majority of residents of Salt Lake City. Respectfully, Lynn K. Pershing, Ph.d President K.E.E.P. Yalecrest "Keep educating and encouraging preservation" Cc: City Council members: Alejandro Puy, Victoria Petro, Chris Warton, Eva Lopez-Chavez, Darin Mano, Dan Dugan, Sarah Young Mayor Mendenhall

subject: RE: (EXTERNAL) Landscaping Confusion
comment: Dear Mr. kimmel I am writing to express my deep disappointment regarding the recent amendments to the City's Landscaping and Buffers rules. As a resident who has diligently followed the guidelines set forth by the Utah Water Savers and participated in the Landscaping Conversion Incentive Program, I find it incredibly disheartening to learn that the very expensive landscaping project we undertook, which was previously approved under the program, may now require additional expenditures to comply with the new regulations. Our project, which aimed to conserve water and contribute to the sustainability efforts of our community, was meticulously planned and executed, with considerable financial investment on our part. However, the recent amendments seem to disregard these efforts and impose further financial burdens on residents who have already contributed to water conservation initiatives. What perplexes me even more is the apparent disparity in priorities reflected by these amendments. While we are being penalized for our proactive measures to conserve water, our neighbor continues to waste water by watering his grass twice a day, resulting in continuous runoff. Such inconsistencies in enforcement not only undermine the integrity of the regulations but also fail to address the urgent issue of water scarcity, particularly in the face of the ongoing drought in Utah. It is deeply concerning that the City Council's decision appears to be out of touch with the current environmental challenges we are facing. Instead of incentivizing and supporting residents who invest in sustainable practices, these amendments seem regressive and punitive. I urge the City Council to reconsider the recent amendments to the Landscaping and Buffers rules and to prioritize policies that encourage and reward water conservation efforts. It is crucial that we work together as a community to address the pressing issue of water scarcity and ensure the long-term sustainability of our city. Thank you for considering my concerns. I look forward to seeing positive changes that reflect the best interests of our community and the environment. Sincerely, Alissa Kean

subject: Soap2Hope
comment: I am writing to share some remarkable insights regarding Soap2Hope homeless street outreach program. Over the past few months, their efforts have yielded profoundly positive effects on both individuals experiencing homelessness and the community at large. First and foremost, their outreach team has succeeded in establishing trust-based relationships with many individuals living on the streets. This rapport has been instrumental in connecting them with essential resources such as shelter, food, healthcare, employment opportunities, and harm reduction services. By meeting people where they are, they have been able to break down barriers and address their immediate needs effectively. Moreover, their outreach efforts have contributed to a significant reduction of health risks to a number of unsheltered individuals in our community. This not only improves their quality of life but also enhances public safety and fosters a more inclusive and compassionate community. Additionally, their outreach program has had a ripple effect on local businesses and residents. By addressing safer habits with drug use in a proactive and compassionate manner, we've seen a decrease in public nuisance complaints and an increase in community cohesion. Businesses have reported feeling safer and more supported, while residents have expressed appreciation for the positive impact on the overall ambiance of their neighborhoods. Furthermore, their program has served as a catalyst for broader systemic change. By actively engaging with individuals experiencing homelessness, we've gained valuable insights into the root causes of homelessness and the barriers to accessing support services. This information has informed advocacy efforts aimed at addressing systemic issues such as affordable housing, mental health care, and substance abuse treatment. In conclusion, the positive effects of their homeless street outreach program are undeniable. Through compassionate engagement, resource coordination, and community collaboration, they are making tangible strides towards ending homelessness and building a more equitable society for all.

subject: Public Parks and Dog Leashes
comment: Hello, I am a resident of Westgate Lofts, which is directly to the south of the Paperbox Lofts. There is a "public urban park" on the south part of Paperbox Lofts, per the SLC RDA. The reality is that it's a mini dog park for Paperbox residents, as well as Westgate. (And eventually for those of Zephyr Lofts.) There seem to be no signs posted indicating it is a public park, or regarding the leash status of dogs. My understanding of city and county ordinances is that, by default, all public spaces require a leash, unless specifically posted otherwise. Unfortunately, many people seem to think that it's private property (I've had a Paperbox resident express this belief to me), or are unaware of the law (or unwilling to follow it). Just today I witnessed a scuffle between dogs (one off leash) where at least one of the dogs yelped in pain at one point. I think the owners had them make up, so no real harm done it seems. Later, when I went to check the signage, I had the unpleasant opportunity of being humped by a husky wearing a pink vest, and an owner who refused to control his dog when asked (he preferred to question my lack of bravery). I've had unleashed dogs rush me when I'm walking nearby, and my wife has had dogs rush her while dog-walking. Would it be possible to have signs posted as to the public nature of the park and city leash laws? I'm not sure if the intended outcome of an urban public park was a doggy bathroom where passersby are consistently at risk of an off-leash dog rushing and/or humping them, but it seems like a bad result if the goal was to make that area a pleasant place for the public to pass through. P.S. Love the new zoning simplification initiative. Best, Lance Spencer, a concerned resident

subject: Public Comments in support of the ESG 2024-2025 grant application Soap2Hope
comment: Good afternoon! My name is Noora Chingaliyeva. I am the Victim/Witness Coordinator at the Utah Attorney General's Office and the Utah Trafficking in Person Task Force, Victim Services Subcommittee Coordinator. I am writing to express my full support for the grant application submitted by Soap2Hope for the Emergency Solutions Grant (ESG). As a partner with Soap2Hope and the Utah Attorney General's Office, I have had the privilege of witnessing firsthand the invaluable contributions that Soap2Hope has made to our community, particularly in the realm of supporting trafficking survivors. Since 2020, Soap2Hope has been an integral partner of the Utah Trafficking in Person Task Force, playing a pivotal role in providing essential services to trafficking survivors. Under the leadership of its founder, January Riggin, Soap2Hope has consistently demonstrated a commitment to excellence and innovation in its approach to service provision. One of the standout qualities of Soap2Hope is its dedication to victim-centered and victim-driven practices. Through its culturally responsive and trauma-informed approach, Soap2Hope ensures that survivors receive the support and resources they need to heal and rebuild their lives. I have personally witnessed the impact of Soap2Hope's trainings and outreach efforts, which have reached diverse audiences, including statewide law enforcement agencies and victim advocates. The partnership between Soap2Hope and the Utah Attorney General's Office has been instrumental in advancing our shared goals of combatting trafficking and supporting survivors. By leveraging Soap2Hope's expertise and resources, we have been able to enhance our efforts in addressing the complex needs of trafficking survivors and improving our overall response to this critical issue. I am confident that a grant awarded to Soap2Hope will enable them to continue their vital work and expand their reach to even more survivors in need. I urge you to consider Soap2Hope's application favorably and provide them with the support they need to continue making a meaningful difference in the lives of trafficking survivors. Please do not hesitate to reach out to me if you have any questions. Sincerely, Noora Chingaliyeva

comment: Hi All, Now that the State has released its "new" plan for how to "help" the homeless in our community, I will once again say what no one wants to hear... Doing more of the same old will help no one. The "new" plan suggests that doubling the size of the shelters, without changing what we do, will somehow make what did not work, work better... Makes sense to me. If something isn't working...do more of it...and continue to pretend it is... How can we start a meaningful conversation about what is or is not working? Bernie Hart

subject: Community Assistance Recovery Funding- Soap2Hope
comment: Hello Council, I want to speak to my belief in and experience supporting Soap2Hope over the last five years, first as a volunteer, then as a board member, and now as a consultant on grant writing and funding strategy. I am the Executive Director of the Utah Peer Network, a non-profit in Salt Lake County. I have been working in the recovery space for the last fifteen years as a clinician and as a peer. January has successfully managed several funding streams to support the work of Soap2Hope, which continues to expand to reach more Salt Lake City residents. Monthly, the number of people they are able to impact increases, and often, they will be a last resort for access to someone who is desperate for some type of recovery assistance. S2H works diligently and recognizes the importance of this funding, which they do not take lightly. The community partnerships and subsequent donations S2H has made fill in the gaps that most small nonprofits do not have access to, which she has garnered through sheer grit and hard work. Her yearly fundraiser and regular donations show her determination to fill in funding streams and responsibly steward those funds. January approaches the community she serves through the lens of lived experience. She holds hope when most will look the other way. Soap2Hope has become a sustainable and viable service to the residents of SLC who are marginalized and who truly do not/or cannot access recovery services in other ways. Please consider keeping Soap2Hope one of the organizations funded through the Emergency Solutions Grant so that it can continue expanding and providing harm reduction (disease prevention, lowered medical costs, community, peer support, syringe exchange, cleanup, and resources) through this unique and ethically run organization. Thank you for your time. Thoughtfully, Lisa
